question: You encounter a complete uterine inversion with the placenta still attached. The MOST IMPORTANT immediate principle regarding the placenta in this situation is:

answers.text: Remove the placenta first to improve access for manual uterine reduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect and DANGEROUS. Removing the placenta before reduction greatly increases haemorrhage by disrupting the placental attachment site before the uterus has been restored to normal anatomy and uterotonic agents can contract it.

answers.text: Leave the placenta in situ and attempt uterine reduction BEFORE placental removal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The cardinal rule is: DO NOT remove the placenta before reducing the uterus. The placenta acts as a tamponade over the placental bed. Remove it only after the uterus has been fully reduced and a uterotonic has been administered to cause uterine contraction.

answers.text: Administer carboprost immediately to contract the uterus around the placenta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Uterotonic agents must NOT be given before reduction — they will cause the cervical ring to contract, trapping the inverted uterus and making reduction impossible. Give uterotonics only AFTER successful reduction.

answers.text: Proceed directly to Huntington's surgical technique without attempting manual reduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Manual reduction (Johnson manoeuvre) should always be attempted first. Surgical techniques (Huntington, Haultain) are reserved for failed manual reduction. Bypass surgery is not appropriate as the initial step.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember the cardinal principle: leave the placenta in place and reduce the uterus first. Removing the placenta beforehand, or giving uterotonics before reduction, can precipitate catastrophic haemorrhage or make reduction impossible.
Well done. The rule is absolute: NEVER remove the placenta before reducing the inverted uterus. Reduction first, then uterotonic, then placental removal.
